record.title: Fixed normalized angles on all sufficiently high-girth regular graphs

aligned_passages.text: ### 11.3 Depth, angle choice and the order of quantifiers The complete witness is a finite ordered word, including every real angle. Its existence for each error tolerance asserts uniformity in system size and disorder that fixed-instance convergence does not provide. The quantifiers should be read literally. The source theorem says that for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is one finite word $W_\varepsilon$ such that $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E E_n(W_\varepsilon)\ge P_*-\varepsilon. $$ The cost operator uses $J,n$, but this word and its angles do not. In fixed-instance QAOA convergence, by contrast, the chosen depth and angles may depend on the fixed finite cost matrix and the requested accuracy. The performance of a prescribed family of nonzero angles with $p=p(n)\to\infty$ needs further estimates. A depth allowance alone can be met by the padded existence construction below. The distinction already occurs for the elementary array $a_{n,p}=p/(n+p)$. For each fixed $n$, its limit as $p\to\infty$ is one; for each fixed $p$, its limit as $n\to\infty$ is zero. This is a quantifier example, not a model of QAOA. The finite-dimensional convergence theorem of [Binkowski, Koßmann, Ziegler and Schwonnek, arXiv:2302.04968v1, Theorem 12][binkowski] fixes the optimization problem before selecting a sufficiently long circuit. It does not replace the construction of a size-independent word here. **An existential schedule under a prescribed depth allowance.** There is a narrower diagonal consequence for sampled output. Choose $W_k$ with $P_*-1/k\le v_{W_k}\le P_*$. Fixed-word second-moment convergence supplies $N_k$ so that, for every $n\ge N_k$, $\mathbb E(E_n(W_k)-v_{W_k})^2\le k^{-2}$. Given any prescribed integer depth allowance $d(n)\to\infty$, enlarge these strictly increasing thresholds until $d(n)\ge\operatorname{depth}(W_k)$ for every $n\ge N_k$. On $N_k\le n **Computational meaning of a finite word.** Nor does a supremum over angles assert that an optimizing angle vector exists at any particular depth. The proof constructs a sufficiently good word directly; monotonicity from identity padding then gives the limit of $Q_p$. Each QAOA round contains a full cost evolution and a mixer evolution. In the dense SK model a cost evolution involves all $\binom n2$ pair couplings, so the round count is not itself a bound on two-qubit gate depth, connectivity cost, precision or physical runtime. Three computational questions remain distinct. Evaluating the limiting energy at supplied angles is one task; finding suitable angles is another; implementing and sampling the resulting quantum circuit is a third. The [Basso et al. iteration][bfmvz] evaluates the fixed-angle limit in $O(p^2 4^p)$ arithmetic time. That is not a bound on the search needed to find the existence theorem's angles. Spin–boson representations provide another route to evaluation. The earlier [Boulebnane et al. mapping, arXiv:2505.07929v2][spin-boson], and the later [mixed-spin decoupling paper, arXiv:2609.40309v1, §§II–III and Supplement S2.1][decoupling], must be distinguished: the latter is a separate work, not the reference called BKL2026 in the original QAOA manuscript. Its fixed-depth mapping and numerical tensor-network performance do not supply an efficient angle-selection theorem for the present construction. Its discussion also gives fixed-word finite-size estimates; the absence of a finite-size rate **in the construction here** is not a claim that the wider literature contains none. **Why the two-spin hypothesis matters.** The statement is specific to the quadratic, zero-field SK model. The pure even higher-spin model has a different thermodynamic-first conclusion. For every even interaction order $q\ge4$, [Basso, Gamarnik, Mei and Zhou, arXiv:2204.10306v2, Theorem 4, (3.15), and its proof in §4.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10306v2) show $$ v_p^{(q)}(\boldsymbol\theta,\boldsymbol\beta) \le\eta_{\mathrm{OGP}}(G_q)<\eta_{\mathrm{OPT}}(G_q) $$ for every finite $p$ and every fixed angle vector, in that source's normalization. The same ceiling bounds their supremum over all finite $p$ and angles. The proof combines its dense–sparse value identity with the coupled-overlap-gap obstruction of [Chou, Love, Sandhu and Shi, arXiv:2108.06049v3, Parameter 4.1 and Corollary 4.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.06049v3). That local-algorithm obstruction applies to sparse random signed Max-$q$-XOR for even $q\ge4$, at sufficiently large fixed degree and under the source's logarithmic-depth bound. The Basso–Gamarnik–Mei–Zhou transfer above only needs the resulting obstruction at each fixed depth. It requires no interchange of depth and system size. The exclusion $q\ge4$ is essential; this is not an obstruction for the SK two-spin model treated here. For comparison, [Goh, arXiv:2404.06087v6, Theorem 4.2 and Corollary 4.2.1][goh], treats even interaction order at least four. Its logarithmic-depth obstruction concerns sparse random-regular Max-q-XORSAT; the dense spin-glass corollary is explicitly conditional on swapping limits. The source states on p. 12 that its sparse/dense equivalence is only established at fixed depth, so it does not prove a dense logarithmic-depth obstruction. These hypotheses do not include quadratic SK. Neither a conclusion for all mixed spin glasses nor a general quantum advantage follows from §8. ### 11.4 The regular-MaxCut consequence has its own limits The original manuscript also gives a consequence for MaxCut. For each $\eta>0$ it selects one finite depth and normalized angles, and then a degree threshold, such that every finite simple unweighted $(D+1)$-regular graph of girth greater than $2p+1$ has expected cut fraction at least $$ \frac12+\frac{P_*-\eta}{\sqrt D} $$ for all sufficiently large $D$. The usual MaxCut cost is $H_{\rm MC}=\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}}(I-Z_iZ_j)$, so its angles are $2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D$: the normalized angles are fixed, while these physical cost angles depend on degree. The sign conversion uses a bipartition of the relevant tree neighbourhood of each edge; the whole graph need not be bipartite. The further optimality comparison is for a uniform simple labelled $(D+1)$-regular graph $G_{n,D+1}$, along sizes with $n(D+1)$ even. Write $\operatorname{OPT}(G)$ for the maximum cut size divided by $|E(G)|$, $q_{p,G}$ for the circuit's expected cut fraction, and $\Delta_D(G)=\operatorname{OPT}(G)-q_{p,G}(2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D, \boldsymbol\beta)$. The same word can be chosen so that $$ \lim_{D\to\infty} \limsup_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n(D+1)\ \mathrm{even}}} \Pr_G\{\sqrt D\,\Delta_D(G_{n,D+1})>\eta\}=0. $$ Size goes to infinity first at fixed degree and word. The probability is over the random graph; the cut fraction has already averaged the quantum measurement. For fixed $D,p$, [McKay, Wormald and Wysocka (2004), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.37236/1819), gives tight counts of cycles of lengths at most $2p+3$. Every edge with a nontree neighbourhood is within bounded distance of one of these cycles, so their fraction tends to zero. The optimum is supplied separately by [Dembo, Montanari and Sen, arXiv:1503.03923v2, Theorem 1.6(b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03923v2): dividing their cut size per vertex by $(D+1)/2$ gives the leading cut fraction $1/2+P_*/\sqrt{D+1}$, with an error $o(D^{-1/2})$ in the stated iterated regime. A high-girth lower bound alone would not prove optimality on every high-girth graph. See [OpenAI (2026b), Corollary 1.2 and its complete proof][q-maxcut]. This separate consequence is recorded to preserve the source's scope; it is not a new selected formal endpoint or a joint size–degree limit.
